tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: propose it and call this.

The result says which case below applies. When the box shows your question, it ends your turn: write no text after this call, since the recap and question say what the user needs and your work above holds the detail. Otherwise your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, with any question the box did not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label and message are the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available now, or one your own work this turn made available; anything else is refused, and one that stops being available later is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and the other answers), so do not guess. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Fix 2 instead", "Not now": a button, not a sentence; the detail goes in message. No "@", no leading / or !. Ignored for an app action (the app's own label is used).

message.description: For a reply: what the click sends, up to 300 characters of plain text — no "@" anywhere, no leading / or !. Omit when the label is the whole message.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

schema.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': path to the built .app bundle (e.g. DerivedData/.../Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the simulator already attached, else the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

title.description: Short snake_case identifier for this visual. Must be specific and disambiguating — if the conversation has multiple visuals, this title alone should tell you which one is being referenced (e.g. 'q4_revenue_by_product_line' not 'chart', 'oauth_login_flow' not 'diagram'). Also used as the download filename, so no spaces or special characters.

widget_code.description: SVG or HTML code to render. For SVG: raw SVG code starting with <svg> tag, must use CSS variables for colors. Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. Use CSS variables for theming. Keep background transparent and avoid top-level padding. Scripts are supported but execute after streaming completes.

## 1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai .../artifact/... link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{...}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

content.content:
**When can an AudioContext start?** The page says Web Audio "has been covered by autoplay since Chrome 71." It recommends waiting for user interaction before starting playback: "wait for a user interaction before starting audio playback." The Web Audio section doesn't list the other conditions from the general autoplay rules, such as Media Engagement on desktop.

**What state is it in before a gesture?** If the AudioContext is created before a user gesture, it starts "suspended." The page says it "will be created in the "suspended" state." To check, read `AudioContext.state` after creation: "If playing is allowed, it should immediately switch to `running`." Otherwise "it will be `suspended`."

**What must the page do?** Yes, the page should call `resume()` after a user gesture. If the context is created on page load, "you will need to call `resume()` after the user gesture." The page also says the context can resume another way: "the `AudioContext` will be resumed after a user gesture if `start()` is called on any attached node." Alternatively, the page can create the AudioContext inside the click handler, so no resume call is needed.

content.content:
Yes, `keydown` counts, with exceptions. To be an activation-triggering input event, an event must:

> *   has the [`isTrusted`] attribute set to `true`, and
> *   is one of the following types:
>     *   `keydown` (except for the Esc key, browser-reserved shortcuts, and certain keys that do not produce user activation, which vary by keyboard, such as Caps Lock, Num Lock, and Print Screen. The behavior may vary by browser.)
>     *   `mousedown`
>     *   `pointerdown` (if `pointerType` is "mouse")
>     *   `pointerup` (if `pointerType` is not "mouse")
>     *   `touchend`

The exceptions for `keydown` are:
- The Esc key
- Browser-reserved shortcuts
- Certain keys that vary by keyboard, such as Caps Lock, Num Lock, and Print Screen

The page notes that behavior may vary by browser.

Because of the `isTrusted` requirement, script-dispatched events (for example, `element.dispatchEvent(new KeyboardEvent("keydown"))`) do not create activation.

**`powerPreference`** (allowed values): "A hint to the user agent indicating what configuration of GPU is suitable for the WebGL context. Possible values are:"

- **`"default"`**: "Let the user agent decide which GPU configuration is most suitable. This is the default value."
- **`"high-performance"`**: "Prioritizes rendering performance over power consumption."
- **`"low-power"`**: "Prioritizes power saving over rendering performance."

**`antialias`**: "A boolean value that indicates whether or not to perform anti-aliasing if possible."

**`preserveDrawingBuffer`**: "If the value is true the buffers will not be cleared and will preserve their values until cleared or overwritten by the author."

The page's own example passes context attributes like this:

```js
const gl = canvas.getContext("webgl", {
  antialias: false,
  depth: false,
});
```

A combined call using the three attributes above (my illustration, not from the page) might look like:

```js
const gl = canvas.getContext("webgl", {
  antialias: true,
  powerPreference: "high-performance",
  preserveDrawingBuffer: false,
});
```

**1. Download from Mixamo**
- Download the base character as FBX with the T-pose: "choosing Format = `FBX`, Pose = `T-pose`".
- Download each animation separately in FBX, without the skin: "Don’t include the skin, because we already have that in the base character file."

**2. Combine in Blender (2.78c)**
- Import the base character and each animation with File → Import → FBX. Use Manual Orientation and Automatic Bone Orientation.
- Name the base object "Character" and its first animation "TPose." Name the other animations to match, such as "Run" and "Idle."
- Preview each action in the Dope Sheet's Action Editor with the character selected.

**3. Export to glTF**
- Delete the extra armatures so only the base character and its armature remain: "Delete the armatures for each animation, leaving only the base character."
- Use either the Khronos or Kupoman glTF exporter, not both. With Khronos, "Ensure the actions you want to export are either active, stashed, or "pushed down" into NLA tracks."
- With Kupoman, set animation export to All Eligible so every clip is included: "This ensures we get all of the available animations, not just the T-Pose."
- Export via File → Export → glTF. The article's output is a `.gltf` file, a `.bin` file, and possibly textures. It does not describe a GLB export.

**4. Play in three.js**
- The article doesn't show AnimationMixer code. It recommends the A-Frame `animation-mixer` component, which wraps the three.js animation system, for quick playback. Example: `animation-mixer="clip: Run;"`.
- For full control, the article points to the three.js animation system docs, noting that `animation-mixer` uses it under the hood.

content.content:
In the "Free the physics" section, the renderer produces time and the simulation consumes it in fixed steps. Each frame adds the elapsed time to the accumulator, "accumulator += frameTime;", and the simulation steps forward only while "while ( accumulator >= dt )", subtracting dt each time. Leftover time carries over to the next frame.

The article's "final touch" then blends the two most recent physics states for display. It computes "const double alpha = accumulator / dt;" and renders "State state = currentState * alpha + previousState * ( 1.0 - alpha );". In my own words, the leftover accumulator shows how far the render time sits between the last and next physics steps, so dividing by dt yields a blend factor from 0 to 1.

cat > $D/doc/partA.md <<'EOF'
# Render track research: Three.js 0.186 split-screen renderer and camera rig

Scope: `src/render/*`, `src/scene/camera.ts`, `src/scene/layout.ts`, `src/scene/hud.ts` (plus `src/scene/minimap.ts`). Everything below was checked against the installed packages in `node_modules` (three 0.186.1, @types/three 0.186.0, typescript 5.9, vitest 5) and against the sources listed in section 6. All TypeScript in section 3 typechecks under the repo's `tsconfig.json` options plus `noUnusedLocals`/`noUnusedParameters`, and the pure parts (layout, camera, map-to-blocks, hull geometry) pass 19 vitest tests. The verification log is in the appendix.

## 1. The problem, in the words of the spec

- "The target is convincing Venice at projector distance, at 60 fps with 4 viewports. Realism comes from light, water and materials far more than from polygon count." (section 9)
- "3D: Three.js, plain (no React in the game loop) ... split screen via scissor viewports" (section 11); "render(state, events, layout) // one camera per team, scissor viewports" (interfaces between tracks); "Timestep: fixed 60 Hz simulation; the renderer interpolates between steps." (section 8)
- Layouts on a 16:9 screen, fixed for the round: 2 teams side by side; 3 teams 2x2 with the spare cell as a live overview map; 4 teams 2x2 with the minimap where the cells meet; 5 teams 3x2 plus overview; 6 teams 3x2 with the minimap at the crossing. "Each viewport has a thick border in the team colour and the team name." (section 2)
- Camera: "Sits about 9 m behind and 4 m above the boat, along the aim direction. It looks level, so the horizon runs through the centre of the view and the boat sits in the lower part of the frame." "A small arrow at the bottom of the viewport shows the bow against the aim direction." Kill-cam: "its cell shows a 5 s kill-cam on the boat that sank it, with a countdown, then cuts back to the respawned boat." (sections 2, 4, 5)
- Look: golden hour, "A warm HDRI sky (Poly Haven, free CC0), a low sun, soft haze in the distance." Water: "dark green-teal with animated normal maps, sky reflection and foam behind moving boats. No mirror-style planar reflections: they double the render cost of every viewport." Buildings generated from the grid with plaster, Istrian stone, algae band, shutters, chimneys. Gondola "long, black, slightly asymmetric hull with the iron bow piece (ferro), trim in the team colour, and one tall lantern at the bow glowing in the team colour". Crew: Mixamo GLB, "If importing eats too much time, use simple stylised characters generated in code ... Decide this in the first hour, not later." (section 9)
- Performance rules: "Share geometry and materials; use instancing for windows, poles and lanterns; merge building meshes per block. Render the shadow map once per frame, not once per viewport. Let the haze hide the far edge; simplify buildings beyond about 120 m. Measure with 4 viewports by the second checkpoint." Cut order: "Cut draw distance, shadows, then building detail." (sections 9, 14)
- The map: "one ASCII grid in shared/map.ts, 8 m per cell, about 50 x 38 cells" (400 x 300 m); "Coordinates: metres, Y up, water surface at y = 0, map origin at the centre. The 2D physics uses (x, z) of the 3D world." (section 7)
- Audio on the scene PC only; HUD per viewport and shared (section 10). Nothing may block Gate 1 ("one phone steers a box boat on the TV").

## 2. Decisions and why (with rejected alternatives)

| # | Decision | Why | Rejected |
|---|---|---|---|
| a1 | One `WebGLRenderer`, `autoClear = false`, one full-canvas `renderer.clear(true, true, false)` with the scissor test OFF, then per team `setViewport` + `setScissor` + `setScissorTest(true)` + `renderer.render(scene, camera)`. | Viewports are disjoint, so one colour+depth clear covers all of them, and the border gaps between cells get the clear colour. `gl.clear` honours the scissor box, so the clear must happen with the test off. Verified: `WebGLRenderer.setViewport/setScissor` take logical pixels and multiply by the pixel ratio (`WebGLRenderer.js` lines 808-858); `WebGLBackground.render` only clears when `renderer.autoClear` is true or the background is a `Color` (`WebGLBackground.js`, `render()`), so with a texture background no hidden per-viewport clear happens. | The official `webgl_multiple_views` example keeps `autoClear = true` and relies on scissored clears per view: fine too, but it clears depth 4 times and leaves the gaps unclear. `ArrayCamera` (one `render()` call, sub-cameras with `.viewport`): culls with the parent camera's frustum (`_frustum.setFromProjectionMatrix` at `WebGLRenderer.js:1687` runs once before the sub-camera loop at lines 1770-1776), which is meaningless for four cameras scattered over the map; also one `background.render` for all. Four canvases: four GL contexts, four copies of every texture. |
| a2 | HUD as a DOM overlay (`position: fixed`, `pointer-events: none`), one absolutely positioned div per cell matching the layout rect, border in the team colour, crosshair as inline SVG, minimap as a `<canvas>` 2D. | Text, borders, countdowns and flashes cost zero draw calls and no texture atlases; CSS animations do the flash; the same `Rect` numbers drive both the GL viewport (y flipped) and the div. DOM writes are change-detected so the hot path is a few `style`/`textContent` sets. | Drawing the HUD in the canvas (sprites or a second orthographic pass): needs a text atlas, a 5th render pass or an orthographic camera per cell, and sprites are one draw call each (`WebGLRenderer.js:1890`, sprites are individual render items). |
| a3 | Layout: integer cell edges `round(i*W/cols)` so cells tile exactly; the GL viewport is the cell inset by the border (6 px at 1080p); minimap = spare cell (3, 5 teams) or a 216 px square at the screen centre (2, 4, 6); a reserved scoreboard band top-centre; per-cell corner widgets are pushed away from reserved rects. | The spec table maps directly: 2 -> 2x1, 3-4 -> 2x2, 5-6 -> 3x2; spare index 3 / 5. At the centre crossing the minimap overlaps three cells' inner corners (bottom-right cell's "top left: team name", etc.), so corner widgets must slide. | Shrinking viewports to make room for a gutter wastes screen; a fixed 3x2 for everything makes 4 teams tiny. |
| a4 | `renderer.setPixelRatio(1)` always; `renderer.setSize(w, h, false)` with CSS size owned by the stylesheet. | 1080p with four cells is 960x540 per cell; the projector is 1:1. An integer DPR also keeps `setViewport` (`.round()`, line 820) and `setRenderTarget(null)` (`.floor()`, lines 3047-3048) in step so no 1 px seam appears after the shadow pass restores the viewport. | DPR 2 on a Retina laptop quadruples the fill with no visible gain on the wall. |
| b | Shadows: ONE static shadow map baked at load (`shadowMap.autoUpdate = false; shadowMap.needsUpdate = true` once), only buildings, bridges, poles and the campanile cast; boats get a blob shadow. A `dynamicShadows` quality flag re-sets `needsUpdate = true` once per frame before the first viewport for the "boats cast" upgrade. 2048^2 orthographic map over +-260 m (0.25 m per texel), `PCFShadowMap`, `bias -0.0004`, `normalBias 0.6`. | Verified in `WebGLShadowMap.js`: `render()` returns early when `autoUpdate === false && needsUpdate === false` (line 95), renders all shadow lights, then `scope.needsUpdate = false` (line 376) at the end of that one call, so viewports 2..4 of the same frame reuse the map. The shadow pass is called from `WebGLRenderer.render()` before the scene draw (line 1737) and renders into the shadow render target, whose own viewport/scissor replace the screen scissor (`setRenderTarget`, lines 3041-3071), so it is not clipped by the current cell. `PCFSoftShadowMap` was removed from the WebGL path in r186 (`WebGLShadowMap.js:100-103` warns and falls back; migration guide r182: "`PCFShadowMap` ... is now soft as well"). A low sun casts long building shadows across the canals: the single biggest "Venice" cue, nearly free when static. | No shadows at all: loses the look for nothing (one baked pass). Per-frame dynamic shadows for everything: + one depth pass per frame of all casters, acceptable but not needed for the MVP; it is the first "shadows" cut. VSM: needs blur passes. |
| c | Lighting: `ACESFilmicToneMapping`, exposure 0.95; `scene.environment` + `scene.background` from a PMREM; procedural `Sky` addon + `PMREMGenerator.fromScene` on frame 1 (no download), then `HDRLoader` (not `RGBELoader`: deprecated since r180, it is now a thin subclass that `console.warn`s) + `fromEquirectangular` for Poly Haven "Venice Sunset" 1K (CC0) swapped in later; one `DirectionalLight` at 14 deg elevation; faint `HemisphereLight` floor. `Fog` (linear) 40..140 m, colour from the HDRI horizon row. Colour management: r186 defaults are `ColorManagement.enabled = true`, `renderer.outputColorSpace = SRGBColorSpace`, textures default to `NoColorSpace`: colour textures must be tagged `SRGBColorSpace`, normal/data maps left alone; `HDRLoader` returns `HalfFloatType` + `LinearSRGBColorSpace`. | Linear fog factor is `smoothstep(near, far, depth)` (`fog_fragment.glsl.js`): 0.35 at 80 m, 0.90 at 120 m, 1.0 at 140 m, which is exactly "hide beyond about 120 m" and lets the per-viewport distance cull at 120-160 m be invisible. Fog is mixed after tone mapping and colour-space conversion (`meshphysical.glsl.js` includes `tonemapping_fragment`, `colorspace_fragment`, then `fog_fragment`) and `WebGLMaterials.refreshFogUniforms` converts `fog.color` to the output colour space, so an sRGB hex fog colour matches what you see. | `FogExp2`: density 0.01265 for 90 % at 120 m, but then 99.995 % at 250 m, so the campanile vanishes; the spec wants it "seen from every viewport". Sky-mesh-only (no HDRI): fine as the fallback, kept. `outputBufferType: HalfFloatType` (new r18x option): routes every render through an internal HDR target plus a copy (`WebGLRenderer.js:565-567, 1659, 1808`); the default `UnsignedByteType` tone-maps in the material shader for free. |
| d | Water: one 1400 m `PlaneGeometry` with `MeshStandardMaterial` (color `0x0f3b38`, roughness 0.22, metalness 0, `envMapIntensity 1`), two scrolling samples of ONE procedurally generated tileable normal map blended in `onBeforeCompile` (replacing `#include <normal_fragment_maps>`, reusing `tbn` from `normal_fragment_begin`), `receiveShadow`, fog on. Foam: a ribbon mesh per boat (`WakeTrail`, ring buffer of stern positions, 28 segments, alpha by age). | Verified the r186 chunk: the tangent-space branch reads `texture2D(normalMap, vNormalMapUv)`, scales by `normalScale`, then `normal = normalize(tbn * mapN)`; my replacement keeps those names so lighting, shadows and fog all still apply. Standard material gives IBL sky reflection from `scene.environment` for free (no extra pass). | `three/addons/objects/Water.js`: a planar mirror (`WebGLRenderTarget`, `mirrorCamera`, `mirrorSampler`), i.e. the scene rendered again per camera; `Water2.js` imports `Reflector` and `Refractor` (two extra renders). Both are exactly the "mirror-style planar reflections" the spec bans; with four viewports they would be 8-12 scene renders per frame. Custom `ShaderMaterial` water: loses shadows/fog/IBL integration, more code. Upgrade path: a foam mask drawn into a small render target (splat the wakes) and sampled in the water shader. |
| e | Buildings: greedy rectangle merge of `B` cells (max 6x6 cells = 48 m so culling stays effective); per rectangle, four stacked `BoxGeometry`s (algae 0.6 m, stone 0.9 m, plaster, cornice) with per-face UVs scaled to metres and a vertex `color` attribute, merged with `mergeGeometries(parts, false)` into ONE mesh with ONE `MeshStandardMaterial({ vertexColors: true, map: grain })`; windows (frame, glass, two shutters), chimneys and mooring poles as `InstancedMesh` per map quadrant with `setColorAt` for shutters; bridges as `ExtrudeGeometry` of a `Shape` with an arch hole (sinus arc, 3.1 m clearance) over `=` runs; the run nearest the centre gets a roof and columns (the covered bridge); `T` is a 70 m campanile whose material keeps 45 % of its colour through the fog. Coordinate convention used everywhere here (to be fixed in `shared/map.ts` by the base phase): world X/Z are the 2D sim axes, Y up, water at y = 0; a yaw `theta` means forward = `(cos theta, 0, sin theta)`; a three.js object modelled with its bow along +X faces that way with `rotation.y = -theta`. Column `c` of the ASCII grid is at `x = (c + 0.5 - cols/2) * 8`, row `r` at `z = (r + 0.5 - rows/2) * 8`.

## 3. Algorithms and code

Each snippet names its target path. The two `shared/*` files are the slice of the contract the renderer needs; they must be merged into the real `shared/map.ts` / `shared/state.ts` (owned by the base phase), not copied beside them. The code imports `@shared/*` through the repo's path alias and `three/addons/*` through three's package exports (also mapped by `@types/three`).

Per-frame algorithm (`renderer.ts`):

1. `timer.update()`; `dt = min(0.1, getDelta())`; `renderer.info.reset()`; if `dynamicShadows` then `shadowMap.needsUpdate = true`.
2. Update visuals from the state: `water.update(time)`; boats (`GondolaView.update(boat, alpha, time, dt)`: interpolation, bob/roll/pitch, sink, wake, crew); pools (`count`, matrices, instance colours); `vfx.onEvents`, `vfx.update`, `audio.onEvents`.
3. `setScissorTest(false); clear(colour, depth)`.
4. For each team `i` with `layout.cells[i]`: `r = toGlViewport(inset(cell, border), layout.height)`; `setViewport(r)`, `setScissor(r)`, `setScissorTest(true)`; `rig.setAspect(r.w / r.h)` (updates `fov` and the projection matrix only when the aspect changed); `updateRig` (follow or kill-cam); `cullByDistance(world.cullables, cameraPos, cullDistance)`; `vfx.setViewport(r.h, fov)`; `renderer.render(scene, rig.camera)`.
5. `setScissorTest(false)`; `perf.sample(...)`; step the quality down if advised.

Layout algorithm (`layout.ts`): `gridFor(n)` -> (cols, rows); cell edges at `round(i * size / n)`; cells in row-major order, the first unused index is the spare cell; `minimap` is the spare cell inset by the border or a `0.2 * min(W, H)` square centred on the screen; `scoreboard` is a `0.34 W x 0.16 H` band at the top centre. `placeWidget(cell, corner, w, h, margin, reserved)` positions a HUD widget at a corner and, while it intersects a reserved rect, pushes it along the axis with the smaller push toward the cell centre (two passes).

Camera rig numbers (`camera.ts`): `verticalFovDeg(aspect) = clamp(2 atan(tan(42.5 deg) / aspect), 50, 75)`; `k = 1 - exp(-lambda dt)` with `lambda = 10` (follow) or 4 (kill-cam); wall march in 0.5 m steps from 2.5 m outward along the boat-to-camera segment, stop one step before the first wall cell.

Water shader replacement (`water.ts`), inserted in place of `#include <normal_fragment_maps>`:

```glsl
vec3 nA = texture2D( normalMap, vNormalMapUv * uScaleA + uTime * uFlowA ).xyz * 2.0 - 1.0;
vec3 nB = texture2D( normalMap, vNormalMapUv * uScaleB + uTime * uFlowB ).xyz * 2.0 - 1.0;
vec3 mapN = normalize( vec3( nA.xy + nB.xy, nA.z * nB.z ) );
mapN.xy *= normalScale;
normal = normalize( tbn * mapN );
```

with `uScaleA = 1400 / 9`, `uScaleB = 1400 / 3.3` (tile sizes in metres over the 1400 m plane) and flows of ~0.02 tiles/s in two directions.

Particle motion (`vfx.ts`, vertex shader): `t = uTime - aBirth`; `k = (1 - exp(-drag t)) / drag` (or `t` when drag is 0); `p = p0 + v k + g t^2 / 2`; `gl_PointSize = min(256, size * (1 + 1.5 age) * H / (2 tan(vfov/2)) / depth)`; alpha fades over the last 45 % of life.

Hull loft (`gondola.ts`): station `s in [0, 1]`, `bulge = sin(pi s)`, `width = 1.4 bulge^0.55`, `depth = 0.5 bulge^0.7 + 0.05`, `yTop = 0.42 + 1.1 (1 - bulge)^3`, keel offset `zc = 0.1 bulge`; profile angle `th in [0, pi]`: `z = zc - (width/2) cos th`, `y = yTop - (yTop + depth) sin th`; quads between neighbouring stations and profile points; a two-vertex deck strip under the gunwale; `computeVertexNormals()`.

Block decomposition (`buildings.ts`): scan row-major; at an unused `B`, grow right while `B` and unused (max 6), then grow down while the whole row segment is `B` and unused (max 6); mark used. Windows go on every 8 m edge segment whose outside neighbour cell is not `B`/`T`, two per segment per floor at +-2 m, floors from `1.5 + 1.9 m` up every 3.3 m; a window is skipped automatically where two merged rectangles touch (the neighbour is `B`). Bridges: runs of `=` along X if `B` sits at both X ends, else along Z; arch hole `y = 3.5 sin(pi t)` over the span minus 1.6 m; extrude depth 5 m centred in the 8 m cell.

## 4. Edge cases and how each is handled

| Case | Handling (where) |
|---|---|
| Team count 2..6 and the spare cell | `computeLayout` clamps to 2..6, spare index = first unused cell (3 teams -> cell 3, 5 teams -> cell 5); tested that cells + spare tile the canvas exactly for 1920x1080 and 1366x768. |
| Odd pixel widths, 3 columns in 1920 px | Edges at `round(i*W/3)` = 0, 640, 1280, 1920: no 1 px gaps or overlaps (test). |
| Minimap or scoreboard overlapping a cell's corner widgets | `placeWidget` slides the widget toward the cell centre (test: bottom-right cell's team name moves >= 108 + 14 px right). |
| Resize / fullscreen / projector plugged in late | `resize()` re-reads `canvas.clientWidth/Height`, `setSize(w, h, false)`; the scene recomputes the layout from the same numbers and calls `hud.setLayout`. Layout is otherwise fixed for the round (spec). |
| Non-integer DPR seams (`round` vs `floor`) | `setPixelRatio(1)` (or the quality tier's 0.75, which then applies to the whole canvas uniformly). |
| Shadow map rebuilt per viewport | `autoUpdate = false`; `needsUpdate` is reset by three at the end of the first shadow pass (`WebGLShadowMap.js:376`), so only one pass per frame even in dynamic mode. If no shadow-casting light is in the render (`lights.length === 0`, line 97) the flag stays set: harmless. Re-enabling shadows after a quality step sets `needsUpdate = true` again. |
| Camera inside a building in an 8 m side canal when the gunner looks sideways | `clampCameraToWater` grid march, min 2.5 m; `near = 0.5`. Fallback if it still clips: building materials are `FrontSide`, so from inside a block you see through its back faces instead of a black screen. |
| Kill-cam when the killer is also dead or unknown (mutual ram, mine owner respawned) | `updateRig` falls back to `follow` on the own (sinking) boat; the HUD shows "SUNK" without a team. |
| Kill-cam -> respawn cut | Mode change back to `follow` clears the smoothed position (`settled = false`), so the camera snaps to the respawn dock instead of flying through walls; the wake and crew are reset on `alive` rising edge or a > 20 m jump. |
| Interpolating across a respawn teleport | `GondolaView.update`: a jump > 20 m between `p*` and current uses `alpha = 1`. Angles use `lerpAngle` (shortest arc) from `shared/math.ts`. |
| Campanile beyond the fog | Linear fog reaches 100 % at 140 m; the campanile's material uses `weakenFog` (fog factor x 0.55) so it stays a 45 % silhouette anywhere on the map; it is never distance-culled; `camera.far = 450` covers the 500 m diagonal. |
| Lantern glow seen through walls | The glow sprite keeps `depthTest` on, so a building hides it, consistent with the hiding rule; it has `fog: false` so it reads at range in the open. |
| `gl_PointSize` limits per GPU | Capped at 256 px; the explosion column is a spray burst plus a glow burst rather than one giant point. |
| InstancedMesh pools and frustum culling | Dynamic pools set `frustumCulled = false`; static instanced meshes call `computeBoundingSphere()` once after the matrices are set. |
| `renderer.info` per render call | `autoReset = false`, one `reset()` per frame; the overlay divides calls by the viewport count. |
| HDRI missing, offline, or slow | The procedural `Sky` + PMREM is built synchronously on startup; `applyHdri` is fire-and-forget after frame 2 and catches errors. Nothing blocks Gate 1. |
| AudioContext suspended | Created lazily in `unlock()` from the Start click / Space keydown; `resume()` if suspended; missing sound files are silently skipped. |
| WebGL context lost | `webglcontextlost` logs and three's `render()` becomes a no-op (`_isContextLost` check at the top of `render()`); the scene shows a reload message. |
| Tab hidden / rAF paused | `Timer` clamps `dt` to 0.1 s in `render()`; the sim loop owns its own accumulator. |
| `scene.background` as a `Color` instead of a texture | `WebGLBackground.render` then force-clears inside the current scissor on every viewport: correct, slightly wasteful; with the PMREM texture no clear happens. |
| Transparent sorting with four cameras | three sorts the render list per `render()` call relative to that camera (`sortObjects`), so wakes, sprites and bubbles sort correctly per viewport. |
| 16-bit index overflow when merging | `BufferGeometry.setIndex` picks `Uint32BufferAttribute` when needed (`arrayNeedsUint32`); blocks are far below the limit anyway (4 boxes, 96 vertices). |
| Water plane edge visible | 1400 m plane, fog at 140 m: the edge is 500 m beyond the fog from any camera on the 400 x 300 map. |
| Shutters/windows cost when triangle-bound | 4.6 k windows x (frame + glass + 2 shutters) as boxes is ~220 k triangles per viewport; the "detail" cut hides them, or swap the box geometries for `PlaneGeometry` quads (12 -> 2 triangles each). |
| Upgrade to three r187 | The migration guide says `setViewport()/setScissor()` stop scaling by the pixel ratio when a render target is bound; our calls target the canvas, unaffected, but worth a re-test. |

## 5. Day-one testing, with and without phones

Without phones (keyboard harness, Track B):

1. `npm run dev`, open `/scene`, press F3 for the perf overlay. The scene main loop should run the sim at 60 Hz with an accumulator and call `renderer.render(state, events, layout, accumulator / dt)`.
2. Layout smoke test: a debug key (suggest `1`..`6`) sets the team count and rebuilds the layout; check borders, the spare-cell map for 3 and 5, the centre minimap for 2, 4, 6, and that the scoreboard band and minimap push the corner widgets.
3. Camera: drive a keyboard boat (WASD) and turn the aim (Q/E as the gyro stand-in): the crosshair stays centred, the horizon stays mid-cell, the bow arrow rotates, the boat sits in the lower part; drive into a side canal and look sideways: the camera pulls in instead of entering the wall.
4. Kill-cam: a debug key sinks the own boat with a chosen killer id; expect the glide to the killer, "SUNK by", a 5 s countdown, then a hard cut to the dock.
5. Shadows: toggle `dynamicShadows` from the perf tier; the overlay's draw calls should rise by one shadow pass only, never by four.
6. Performance gate (Gate 2 as the spec says): 4 teams, 4 keyboard boats, read the overlay: target >= 55 fps, <= 250 calls per viewport. If below: F4 steps the quality tier (cull distance, shadows, detail, pixel ratio) and the overlay confirms the drop.
7. Unit tests: `npm test` runs `tests/layout.test.ts`, `tests/camera.test.ts`, `tests/buildings.test.ts` (pure functions; 19 assertions pass in the scratch copy).
8. Procedural assets: nothing to download; the HDRI (`public/assets/textures/venice_sunset_1k.hdr`) and sounds (`public/assets/sounds/*.ogg`) are optional and lazy; confirm the console warns but the game runs when they are absent.

With phones (after Gate 1):

1. One iPhone steering through the tunnel: the boat should turn in the viewport with the camera following the boat (aim = yaw until a gunner joins).
2. A second phone as Gunner: the view turns while the boat keeps heading; the bow arrow shows the difference; recentre snaps the arrow to 0.

# Render track research: Three.js 0.186 split-screen renderer and camera rig

Scope: `src/render/*`, `src/scene/camera.ts`, `src/scene/layout.ts`, `src/scene/hud.ts` (plus `src/scene/minimap.ts`). Everything below was checked against the installed packages in `node_modules` (three 0.186.1, @types/three 0.186.0, typescript 5.9, vitest 5) and against the sources listed in section 6. All TypeScript in section 3 typechecks under the repo's `tsconfig.json` options plus `noUnusedLocals`/`noUnusedParameters`, and the pure parts (layout, camera, map-to-blocks, hull geometry) pass 19 vitest tests. The verification log is in the appendix.

## 1. The problem, in the words of the spec

- "The target is convincing Venice at projector distance, at 60 fps with 4 viewports. Realism comes from light, water and materials far more than from polygon count." (section 9)
- "3D: Three.js, plain (no React in the game loop) ... split screen via scissor viewports" (section 11); "render(state, events, layout) // one camera per team, scissor viewports" (interfaces between tracks); "Timestep: fixed 60 Hz simulation; the renderer interpolates between steps." (section 8)
- Layouts on a 16:9 screen, fixed for the round: 2 teams side by side; 3 teams 2x2 with the spare cell as a live overview map; 4 teams 2x2 with the minimap where the cells meet; 5 teams 3x2 plus overview; 6 teams 3x2 with the minimap at the crossing. "Each viewport has a thick border in the team colour and the team name." (section 2)
- Camera: "Sits about 9 m behind and 4 m above the boat, along the aim direction. It looks level, so the horizon runs through the centre of the view and the boat sits in the lower part of the frame." "A small arrow at the bottom of the viewport shows the bow against the aim direction." Kill-cam: "its cell shows a 5 s kill-cam on the boat that sank it, with a countdown, then cuts back to the respawned boat." (sections 2, 4, 5)
- Look: golden hour, "A warm HDRI sky (Poly Haven, free CC0), a low sun, soft haze in the distance." Water: "dark green-teal with animated normal maps, sky reflection and foam behind moving boats. No mirror-style planar reflections: they double the render cost of every viewport." Buildings generated from the grid with plaster, Istrian stone, algae band, shutters, chimneys. Gondola "long, black, slightly asymmetric hull with the iron bow piece (ferro), trim in the team colour, and one tall lantern at the bow glowing in the team colour". Crew: Mixamo GLB, "If importing eats too much time, use simple stylised characters generated in code ... Decide this in the first hour, not later." (section 9)
- Performance rules: "Share geometry and materials; use instancing for windows, poles and lanterns; merge building meshes per block. Render the shadow map once per frame, not once per viewport. Let the haze hide the far edge; simplify buildings beyond about 120 m. Measure with 4 viewports by the second checkpoint." Cut order: "Cut draw distance, shadows, then building detail." (sections 9, 14)
- The map: "one ASCII grid in shared/map.ts, 8 m per cell, about 50 x 38 cells" (400 x 300 m); "Coordinates: metres, Y up, water surface at y = 0, map origin at the centre. The 2D physics uses (x, z) of the 3D world." (section 7)
- Audio on the scene PC only; HUD per viewport and shared (section 10). Nothing may block Gate 1 ("one phone steers a box boat on the TV").

| # | Decision | Why | Rejected |
|---|---|---|---|
| a1 | One `WebGLRenderer`, `autoClear = false`, one full-canvas `renderer.clear(true, true, false)` with the scissor test OFF, then per team `setViewport` + `setScissor` + `setScissorTest(true)` + `renderer.render(scene, camera)`. | Viewports are disjoint, so one colour+depth clear covers all of them, and the border gaps between cells get the clear colour. `gl.clear` honours the scissor box, so the clear must happen with the test off. Verified: `WebGLRenderer.setViewport/setScissor` take logical pixels and multiply by the pixel ratio (`WebGLRenderer.js` lines 808-858); `WebGLBackground.render` only clears when `renderer.autoClear` is true or the background is a `Color` (`WebGLBackground.js`, `render()`), so with a texture background no hidden per-viewport clear happens. | The official `webgl_multiple_views` example keeps `autoClear = true` and relies on scissored clears per view: fine too, but it clears depth 4 times and leaves the gaps unclear. `ArrayCamera` (one `render()` call, sub-cameras with `.viewport`): culls with the parent camera's frustum (`_frustum.setFromProjectionMatrix` at `WebGLRenderer.js:1687` runs once before the sub-camera loop at lines 1770-1776), which is meaningless for four cameras scattered over the map; also one `background.render` for all. Four canvases: four GL contexts, four copies of every texture. |
| a2 | HUD as a DOM overlay (`position: fixed`, `pointer-events: none`), one absolutely positioned div per cell matching the layout rect, border in the team colour, crosshair as inline SVG, minimap as a `<canvas>` 2D. | Text, borders, countdowns and flashes cost zero draw calls and no texture atlases; CSS animations do the flash; the same `Rect` numbers drive both the GL viewport (y flipped) and the div. | a3 | Layout: integer cell edges `round(i*W/cols)` so cells tile exactly; the GL viewport is the cell inset by the border (6 px at 1080p); minimap = spare cell (3, 5 teams) or a 216 px square at the screen centre (2, 4, 6); a reserved scoreboard band top-centre; per-cell corner widgets are pushed away from reserved rects. | The spec table maps directly: 2 -> 2x1, 3-4 -> 2x2, 5-6 -> 3x2; spare index 3 / 5. Coordinate convention used everywhere here (to be fixed in `shared/map.ts` by the base phase): world X/Z are the 2D sim axes, Y up, water at y = 0; a yaw `theta` means forward = `(cos theta, 0, sin theta)`; a three.js object modelled with its bow along +X faces that way with `rotation.y = -theta`. Column `c` of the ASCII grid is at `x = (c + 0.5 - cols/2) * 8`, row `r` at `z = (r + 0.5 - rows/2) * 8`.

## 3. Algorithms and code

Each snippet names its target path. The two `shared/*` files are the slice of the contract the renderer needs; they must be merged into the real `shared/map.ts` / `shared/state.ts` (owned by the base phase), not copied beside them. The code imports `@shared/*` through the repo's path alias and `three/addons/*` through three's package exports (also mapped by `@types/three`).

Per-frame algorithm (`renderer.ts`):

1. `timer.update()`; `dt = min(0.1, getDelta())`; `renderer.info.reset()`; if `dynamicShadows` then `shadowMap.needsUpdate = true`.
2. Update visuals from the state: `water.update(time)`; boats (`GondolaView.update(boat, alpha, time, dt)`: interpolation, bob/roll/pitch, sink, wake, crew); pools (`count`, matrices, instance colours); `vfx.onEvents`, `vfx.update`, `audio.onEvents`.
3. `setScissorTest(false); clear(colour, depth)`.
4. For each team `i` with `layout.cells[i]`: `r = toGlViewport(inset(cell, border), layout.height)`; `setViewport(r)`, `setScissor(r)`, `setScissorTest(true)`; `rig.setAspect(r.w / r.h)` (updates `fov` and the projection matrix only when the aspect changed); `updateRig` (follow or kill-cam); `cullByDistance(world.cullables, cameraPos, cullDistance)`; `vfx.setViewport(r.h, fov)`; `renderer.render(scene, rig.camera)`.
5. `setScissorTest(false)`; `perf.sample(...)`; step the quality down if advised.

Layout algorithm (`layout.ts`): `gridFor(n)` -> (cols, rows); cell edges at `round(i * size / n)`; cells in row-major order, the first unused index is the spare cell; `minimap` is the spare cell inset by the border or a `0.2 * min(W, H)` square centred on the screen; `scoreboard` is a `0.34 W x 0.16 H` band at the top centre. `placeWidget(cell, corner, w, h, margin, reserved)` positions a HUD widget at a corner and, while it intersects a reserved rect, pushes it along the axis with the smaller push toward the cell centre (two passes).

Camera rig numbers (`camera.ts`): `verticalFovDeg(aspect) = clamp(2 atan(tan(42.5 deg) / aspect), 50, 75)`; `k = 1 - exp(-lambda dt)` with `lambda = 10` (follow) or 4 (kill-cam); wall march in 0.5 m steps from 2.5 m outward along the boat-to-camera segment, stop one step before the first wall cell.

Water shader replacement (`water.ts`), inserted in place of `#include <normal_fragment_maps>`:

```glsl
vec3 nA = texture2D( normalMap, vNormalMapUv * uScaleA + uTime * uFlowA ).xyz * 2.0 - 1.0;
vec3 nB = texture2D( normalMap, vNormalMapUv * uScaleB + uTime * uFlowB ).xyz * 2.0 - 1.0;
vec3 mapN = normalize( vec3( nA.xy + nB.xy, nA.z * nB.z ) );
mapN.xy *= normalScale;
normal = normalize( tbn * mapN );
```

with `uScaleA = 1400 / 9`, `uScaleB = 1400 / 3.3` (tile sizes in metres over the 1400 m plane) and flows of ~0.02 tiles/s in two directions.

Particle motion (`vfx.ts`, vertex shader): `t = uTime - aBirth`; `k = (1 - exp(-drag t)) / drag` (or `t` when drag is 0); `p = p0 + v k + g t^2 / 2`; `gl_PointSize = min(256, size * (1 + 1.5 age) * H / (2 tan(vfov/2)) / depth)`; alpha fades over the last 45 % of life.

Hull loft (`gondola.ts`): station `s in [0, 1]`, `bulge = sin(pi s)`, `width = 1.4 bulge^0.55`, `depth = 0.5 bulge^0.7 + 0.05`, `yTop = 0.42 + 1.1 (1 - bulge)^3`, keel offset `zc = 0.1 bulge`; profile angle `th in [0, pi]`: `z = zc - (width/2) cos th`, `y = yTop - (yTop + depth) sin th`; quads between neighbouring stations and profile points; a two-vertex deck strip under the gunwale; `computeVertexNormals()`.

Block decomposition (`buildings.ts`): scan row-major; at an unused `B`, grow right while `B` and unused (max 6), then grow down while the whole row segment is `B` and unused (max 6); mark used. Windows go on every 8 m edge segment whose outside neighbour cell is not `B`/`T`, two per segment per floor at +-2 m, floors from `1.5 + 1.9 m` up every 3.3 m; a window is skipped automatically where two merged rectangles touch (the neighbour is `B`). Bridges: runs of `=` along X if `B` sits at both X ends, else along Z; arch hole `y = 3.5 sin(pi t)` over the span minus 1.6 m; extrude depth 5 m centred in the 8 m cell.

## 4. Edge cases and how each is handled

| Case | Handling (where) |
|---|---|
| Team count 2..6 and the spare cell | `computeLayout` clamps to 2..6, spare index = first unused cell (3 teams -> cell 3, 5 teams -> cell 5); tested that cells + spare tile the canvas exactly for 1920x1080 and 1366x768. |
| Odd pixel widths, 3 columns in 1920 px | Edges at `round(i*W/3)` = 0, 640, 1280, 1920: no 1 px gaps or overlaps (test). |
| Minimap or scoreboard overlapping a cell's corner widgets | `placeWidget` slides the widget toward the cell centre (test: bottom-right cell's team name moves >= 108 + 14 px right). |
| Resize / fullscreen / projector plugged in late | `resize()` re-reads `canvas.clientWidth/Height`, `setSize(w, h, false)`; the scene recomputes the layout from the same numbers and calls `hud.setLayout`. Layout is otherwise fixed for the round (spec). |
| Non-integer DPR seams (`round` vs `floor`) | `setPixelRatio(1)` (or the quality tier's 0.75, which then applies to the whole canvas uniformly). |
| Shadow map rebuilt per viewport | `autoUpdate = false`; `needsUpdate` is reset by three at the end of the first shadow pass (`WebGLShadowMap.js:376`), so only one pass per frame even in dynamic mode. If no shadow-casting light is in the render (`lights.length === 0`, line 97) the flag stays set: harmless. Re-enabling shadows after a quality step sets `needsUpdate = true` again. |
| Camera inside a building in an 8 m side canal when the gunner looks sideways | `clampCameraToWater` grid march, min 2.5 m; `near = 0.5`. Fallback if it still clips: building materials are `FrontSide`, so from inside a block you see through its back faces instead of a black screen. |
| Kill-cam when the killer is also dead or unknown (mutual ram, mine owner respawned) | `updateRig` falls back to `follow` on the own (sinking) boat; the HUD shows "SUNK" without a team. |
| Kill-cam -> respawn cut | Mode change back to `follow` clears the smoothed position (`settled = false`), so the camera snaps to the respawn dock instead of flying through walls; the wake and crew are reset on `alive` rising edge or a > 20 m jump. |
| Interpolating across a respawn teleport | `GondolaView.update`: a jump > 20 m between `p*` and current uses `alpha = 1`. Angles use `lerpAngle` (shortest arc) from `shared/math.ts`. |
| Campanile beyond the fog | Linear fog reaches 100 % at 140 m; the campanile's material uses `weakenFog` (fog factor x 0.55) so it stays a 45 % silhouette anywhere on the map; it is never distance-culled; `camera.far = 450` covers the 500 m diagonal. |
| Lantern glow seen through walls | The glow sprite keeps `depthTest` on, so a building hides it, consistent with the hiding rule; it has `fog: false` so it reads at range in the open. |
| `gl_PointSize` limits per GPU | Capped at 256 px; the explosion column is a spray burst plus a glow burst rather than one giant point. |
| InstancedMesh pools and frustum culling | Dynamic pools set `frustumCulled = false`; static instanced meshes call `computeBoundingSphere()` once after the matrices are set. |
| `renderer.info` per render call | `autoReset = false`, one `reset()` per frame; the overlay divides calls by the viewport count. |
| HDRI missing, offline, or slow | The procedural `Sky` + PMREM is built synchronously on startup; `applyHdri` is fire-and-forget after frame 2 and catches errors. Nothing blocks Gate 1. |
| AudioContext suspended | Created lazily in `unlock()` from the Start click / Space keydown; `resume()` if suspended; missing sound files are silently skipped. |
| WebGL context lost | `webglcontextlost` logs and three's `render()` becomes a no-op (`_isContextLost` check at the top of `render()`); the scene shows a reload message. |
| Tab hidden / rAF paused | `Timer` clamps `dt` to 0.1 s in `render()`; the sim loop owns its own accumulator. |
| `scene.background` as a `Color` instead of a texture | `WebGLBackground.render` then force-clears inside the current scissor on every viewport: correct, slightly wasteful; with the PMREM texture no clear happens. |
| Transparent sorting with four cameras | three sorts the render list per `render()` call relative to that camera (`sortObjects`), so wakes, sprites and bubbles sort correctly per viewport. |
| 16-bit index overflow when merging | `BufferGeometry.setIndex` picks `Uint32BufferAttribute` when needed (`arrayNeedsUint32`); blocks are far below the limit anyway (4 boxes, 96 vertices). |
| Water plane edge visible | 1400 m plane, fog at 140 m: the edge is 500 m beyond the fog from any camera on the 400 x 300 map. |
| Shutters/windows cost when triangle-bound | 4.6 k windows x (frame + glass + 2 shutters) as boxes is ~220 k triangles per viewport; the "detail" cut hides them, or swap the box geometries for `PlaneGeometry` quads (12 -> 2 triangles each). |
| Upgrade to three r187 | The migration guide says `setViewport()/setScissor()` stop scaling by the pixel ratio when a render target is bound; our calls target the canvas, unaffected, but worth a re-test. |

## 5. Day-one testing, with and without phones

Without phones (keyboard harness, Track B):

1. `npm run dev`, open `/scene`, press F3 for the perf overlay. The scene main loop should run the sim at 60 Hz with an accumulator and call `renderer.render(state, events, layout, accumulator / dt)`.
2. Layout smoke test: a debug key (suggest `1`..`6`) sets the team count and rebuilds the layout; check borders, the spare-cell map for 3 and 5, the centre minimap for 2, 4, 6, and that the scoreboard band and minimap push the corner widgets.
3. Camera: drive a keyboard boat (WASD) and turn the aim (Q/E as the gyro stand-in): the crosshair stays centred, the horizon stays mid-cell, the bow arrow rotates, the boat sits in the lower part; drive into a side canal and look sideways: the camera pulls in instead of entering the wall.
4. Kill-cam: a debug key sinks the own boat with a chosen killer id; expect the glide to the killer, "SUNK by", a 5 s countdown, then a hard cut to the dock.

6. Performance gate (Gate 2 as the spec says): 4 teams, 4 keyboard boats, read the overlay: target >= 55 fps, <= 250 calls per viewport. If below: F4 steps the quality tier (cull distance, shadows, detail, pixel ratio) and the overlay confirms the drop.
7. Unit tests: `npm test` runs `tests/layout.test.ts`, `tests/camera.test.ts`, `tests/buildings.test.ts` (pure functions; 19 assertions pass in the scratch copy).
8. Procedural assets: nothing to download; the HDRI (`public/assets/textures/venice_sunset_1k.hdr`) and sounds (`public/assets/sounds/*.ogg`) are optional and lazy; confirm the console warns but the game runs when they are absent.

With phones (after Gate 1):

1. One iPhone steering through the tunnel: the boat should turn in the viewport with the camera following the boat (aim = yaw until a gunner joins).
2. A second phone as Gunner: the view turns while the boat keeps heading; the bow arrow shows the difference; recentre snaps the arrow to 0.
3. Fire: muzzle flash and boom at the firing boat, splash or explosion at the impact; crosshair flashes X on a kill; the kill feed and scoreboard update.
4. Pickup a crate: sparkle and chime; the crate hides and comes back after 8 s.
5. Hull water (Engineer): the boat sits lower and the water bar fills; shake to bail: the engineer swings the bucket.
